content.title: About
content.content: Cow head is a meat portion that includes the brain, cheeks, tongue and other organs. It is widely used in traditional cuisines around the world for soups, pâtés, roasts and charcuterie. The meat is rich in collagen and has a deep, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cow head is considered a delicacy in many Eastern European and Asian cuisines.
The brain and cheeks are high in gelatin, which creates a rich broth when simmered slowly.
Tongue is often prepared separately, marinated and grilled.
Traditional Russian "head" soup is made from the whole head with vegetables and spices.
In the United States, parts of the head are used to make head cheese and other sausages.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Head meat provides high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of collagen
items.content: Gelatinous parts supply collagen, supporting skin, joint and connective‑tissue health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, important for nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Provides iron, zinc and phosphorus, which aid blood formation and bone health.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: Compared with many other cuts, head meat has a moderate amount of fat when prepared without added oils.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: The head can harbor blood residues and bacteria, so it must be thoroughly cleaned and cooked to a safe internal temperature.

items.title: High cholesterol
items.content: Certain parts, especially the brain, are high in cholesterol, so people with cardiovascular concerns should limit intake.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beef.

items.title: Digestive sensitivity
items.content: Large amounts of gelatinous tissue can cause stomach discomfort in people with sensitive digestion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The head can be simmered for 3–4 hours to make a rich broth, then the meat is removed from the bones for soups, stews or roasts. Cheeks are often pan‑fried or braised with vegetables. The brain can be quickly sautéed or made into a pâté. Tongue is usually boiled, peeled and sliced thin for salads or hot dishes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh head in the refrigerator at 0–2 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze it in an airtight bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Before cooking, rinse well and trim excess fat and blood.

content.title: About
content.content: Sprouted wheat bread is a whole‑grain loaf made from wheat kernels that have been allowed to germinate. Sprouting boosts the levels of vitamins, minerals and enzymes, making the bread more nutritious and easier to digest. It has a soft crumb, a subtle nutty aroma and a golden crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sprouted grains contain 2–3 times more B‑vitamins than raw grains.
Antioxidant levels, such as phenolic compounds, increase during sprouting.
This bread is popular in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern diets for its digestibility.
Sprouting reduces phytic acid, improving mineral absorption.
Traditional recipes date back centuries in regions around the Mediterranean Sea.

items.title: Rich in vitamins and minerals
items.content: Sprouted wheat provides higher amounts of B1, B2, B3, as well as magnesium, zinc and iron compared with regular wheat.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Enzymes formed during sprouting help break down starches and proteins more efficiently.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The slower release of carbohydrates leads to a milder rise in blood sugar.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Both soluble and insoluble fiber promote healthy gut function and increase satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Phenolics and vitamin E protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease may react to this bread.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Sprouted wheat bread still contains gluten and is not suitable for a gluten‑free diet.

items.title: Shelf‑life
items.content: Higher moisture can cause faster spoilage; proper storage is essential.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sprouted wheat bread works well toasted, as a sandwich base, alongside soups, or crumbled into salads. It can be grilled, used for breadcrumbs, or paired with spreads and cheeses.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the loaf in a paper bag or cloth sack at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, refrigerate in an airtight container for up to a week or freeze in portions.

coffee-instant-pre-sweetened-with-sugar-.title: Instant Coffee, Pre‑Sweetened with Sugar, Not Reconstituted

content.title: About
content.content: Instant coffee that is pre‑sweetened with sugar does not require any additional water to become a ready‑to‑drink beverage. It is made from roasted coffee beans, from which a flavorful extract is obtained and then dried by freeze‑drying or spray‑drying, with sugar added for instant sweetness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial instant coffee was patented in the early 20th century.
Pre‑sweetened instant coffee is popular in military rations and backpacking meals because of its convenience.
Sugar masks bitterness and creates a smoother taste profile.
Freeze‑drying preserves more aromatic compounds than traditional drying methods.
Instant coffee can contain up to 30 % of the caffeine found in an equivalent amount of ground coffee.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Coffee is rich in polyphenols, which help combat free radicals in the body.

items.title: Improves alertness
items.content: Caffeine enhances vigilance and may temporarily boost cognitive performance.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Caffeine can increase metabolic rate, aiding calorie burning.

items.title: Reduced risk of certain diseases
items.content: Moderate, regular coffee consumption is associated with lower risk of Parkinson’s disease and some cancers.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar provides an immediate source of glucose, useful during intense physical activity.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive intake may contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of type‑2 diabetes.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Large doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Coffee allergy
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience allergic reactions to coffee components.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Coffee can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcer disease.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Prepare by adding a measured scoop of the product to hot water (about 200 ml) and stirring. It can also be used as a sweetener in desserts, sauces, or cocktails.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package, protected from moisture and direct sunlight. After opening, use within 3‑6 months for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Fudgesicle is a frozen dessert pop on a stick made from creamy ice cream flavored like fudge. It is coated with a thin chocolate shell and often contains bits of nuts or caramel. The treat is popular as a refreshing sweet snack in warm weather.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first fudgesicle appeared in the United States in the 1970s as an experimental version of the classic popsicle.
The name combines “fudge” and “popsicle.”
Original recipes used real fudge paste, but today many manufacturers use flavorings.
Fudgesicles are typically sold in bite‑size portions that are easy to hold without a spoon.
Some countries now offer a vegan version made with coconut milk.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy base provides calcium, essential for bone health.

items.title: Contains vitamin A
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision and the immune system.

items.title: Quick energy source
items.content: Sugar and fat give a rapid boost of energy, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Probiotic content (in some versions)
items.content: Certain recipes include live cultures that may benefit gut health.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The dairy base may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Nut allergy
items.content: Some varieties contain nuts, posing a risk for allergic individuals.

items.title: Brain freeze
items.content: Eating it straight from the freezer can cause a sudden headache known as brain freeze.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fudgesicles are eaten directly from the freezer, holding the stick. Letting it sit for a minute allows the chocolate coating to soften. Serve with fresh berries or sprinkle with nut crumble for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower in the original packaging. Over long periods sugar may crystallize, making the texture slightly grainy.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef Gravy, Fat Free (1919) is a ready‑to‑use sauce made from beef broth, thickened without added fats. It delivers a rich meaty flavor and aromatic spices while fitting low‑fat dietary plans.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The product was formulated for people who want the taste of beef without the fat.
Ingredients include only beef broth, natural flavorings, spices, and a fat‑free thickener.
Fat‑free gravy is commonly used in diet cooking as a substitute for traditional butter‑based sauces.
It can be heated in a microwave or on the stovetop in 2‑3 minutes.
The lack of fat gives it a longer shelf life compared to regular gravies.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: No added fats make this gravy suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Beef broth provides a modest amount of protein that helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef is a good source of heme iron, which is readily absorbed by the body.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: Calorie content is significantly lower than that of traditional butter‑based gravies.

items.title: No trans fats
items.content: The absence of fats eliminates trans‑fat content, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Beef allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to beef or to the spices used in the product.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Like many ready sauces, it can contain a relatively high amount of salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Monosodium glutamate
items.content: Flavor enhancers such as MSG may be present, which can cause sensitivity in certain consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add the gravy to boiled potatoes, vegetables, lean meats, or use it as a base for soups. Heat in a saucepan or microwave, stirring to prevent lumps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in the original packaging. After opening, keep refrigerated and use within 5‑7 days. Discard if an off‑odor or discoloration develops.

other-vegetables-as-ingredient-in-omelet.title: Other Vegetables as Ingredient in Omelet

content.title: About
content.content: Vegetables used in an omelet can include bell pepper, tomato, onion, spinach, mushrooms and other fresh or frozen vegetables. They add bright colour, aroma and extra nutrition, making the omelet more filling and wholesome.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Vegetable omelets are a classic breakfast in many countries, from France to Japan.
Combining eggs with vegetables increases the bioavailability of some vitamins, such as beta‑carotene from carrots.
Vegetables in an omelet are a quick way to use leftovers, reducing food waste.
Dark leafy greens like spinach are rich in iron and folate.
Adding fresh herbs (parsley, dill) boosts flavour without extra salt.

items.title: Rich source of vitamins
items.content: Vegetables provide vitamin C, vitamin A (beta‑carotene) and B‑vitamins, supporting immunity and vision.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from vegetables improves gut motility and promotes satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Phytonutrients such as lutein and quercetin help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie nutrient boost
items.content: Vegetables add volume to the dish without significantly increasing calories, useful for weight management.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Potassium and magnesium in vegetables help maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Allergy to specific vegetables
items.content: Some individuals may react to tomatoes, peppers or mushrooms; be aware of personal intolerances.

items.title: Potential food toxins
items.content: Certain raw vegetables (e.g., potatoes) contain solanine and should be cooked before adding to an omelet.

items.title: Digestive discomfort from excess raw veg
items.content: Large amounts of raw vegetables can cause gas and bloating.

items.title: Salt control
items.content: Pre‑seasoned vegetable mixes may already contain salt; adjust seasoning accordingly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dice the vegetables into small pieces and lightly sauté in a little oil for 2‑3 minutes until softened. Pour beaten eggs over the veggies, stir gently and cook to the desired doneness. Finish with fresh herbs if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh vegetables in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer, loosely packed in a perforated bag. Frozen vegetables keep up to 12 months in the freezer. Cooked omelet is best eaten within 2‑3 hours; leftovers can be refrigerated for up to 24 hours.

peas-and-carrots-canned-cooked-fat-added.title: Peas and carrots, canned, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Peas and carrots in cans are a ready‑to‑eat vegetable mix that has been blanched and sealed in oil. The product retains most of the flavor and nutrients of the fresh vegetables, while the added fat makes it more caloric and gives a creamy taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Canning allows the vegetables to be stored for several years without quality loss.
Peas are a good source of plant protein, and carrots provide provitamin A (beta‑carotene).
The pea‑carrot combination is traditional in many cuisines as a nutritious side dish.
Adding fat improves the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins such as A and E.
Canned mixes are often used in baby foods and in diets where cooking facilities are limited.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peas contain about 5 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Carrots provide a high amount of beta‑carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A for eye health.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: The vegetables retain some fiber, which aids normal digestion.

items.title: Fat enhances vitamin absorption
items.content: The added oil helps the body better absorb fat‑soluble vitamins A and E.

items.title: Low sodium when unsalted
items.content: Choosing a no‑salt version provides minerals without excess sodium.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Added oil increases the energy density, so portion size should be monitored.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergic reaction to peas.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Certain canned versions contain salt; people watching sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some products may contain additives; opt for preservative‑free versions if preferred.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The canned peas and carrots can be eaten cold in salads, added to soups, stews, or used as a side dish for meat and fish. They can also be gently warmed in a pan with a pinch of spices.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the unopened can in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days, discarding if any off‑odors or signs of spoilage appear.
